We propose Language-Guided 005 Temporal Token Pruning (LGTTP), which ex- 006 tracts temporal cues from queries to adap- 007 tively assign pruning rates across video frames, 008 preserving contextual continuity while reduc- 009 ing computational overhead. Unlike existing 010 methods that apply uniform token pruning or 011 disruptive keyframe selection, LGTTP main- 012 tains higher token density in temporally rele- 013 vant segments. Our model-agnostic approach 014 integrates with TimeChat and LLaVA-Video 015 architectures, demonstrating substantial efﬁ- 016 ciency gains across diverse benchmarks. Ex- 017 periments show LGTTP reduces computation 018 by 65% while preserving 97-99% of orig- 019 inal performance. On highlight detection, 020 LGTTP achieves +9.5% HIT@1 on QVHigh- 021 lights compared to baseline methods, and 022 for temporal grounding, it maintains 99.6% 023 of original R@1 on Charades-STA. LGTTP 024 shows particular strength for queries with ex- 025 plicit temporal markers while remaining effec- 026 tive for general video understanding tasks. 027 1 Introduction 028 Vision Language Models like TimeChat (Ren 029 et al., 2024), LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024), 030 and VideoLLaVA (Lin et al., 2023) have demon- 031 strated exceptional capabilities across various 032 video understanding tasks, from highlight detec- 033 tion to temporal grounding and video question an- 034 swering. However, these models face substantial 035 computational inefﬁciency when processing long- 036 form videos, as they typically encode every frame 037 into visual tokens and process the entire token se- 038 quence for each query. The computational com- 039 plexity grows quadratically with sequence length 040 due to the attention mechanism, making efﬁcient 041 token management a critical challenge for practi- 042 cal deployment. Real-world video queries often 043 target speciﬁc temporal segments, making full se- 044 quence processing inefﬁcient. 045 Current efﬁciency approaches fall into two cat- 046 egories with signiﬁcant limitations: (1) vision to- 047 ken pruning methods like PruMerge (Shang et al., 048 2024) and ToMe (Bolya et al., 2023), which re- 049 duce spatial redundancy within individual frames 050 but fail to capture temporal connections; and (2) 051 keyframe selection methods like KeyVideoLLM 052 (Liang et al., 2024) and VideoTree (Wang et al., 053 2024), which disrupt temporal context by com- 054 pletely discarding intermediate frames. These lim- 055 itations are particularly problematic for temporal 056 understanding tasks that rely on maintaining tem- 057 poral coherence across frames, such as highlight 058 detection and temporal grounding. 059 We propose Language-Guided Temporal Token 060 Pruning (LGTTP), a model-agnostic approach that 061 addresses these limitations by adaptively assign- 062 ing pruning rates based on temporal cues extracted 063 from queries. LGTTP integrates effectively with 064 both TimeChat and LLaVA-Video architectures, 065 showing particular strength with models that have 066 built-in temporal awareness. By leveraging tem- 067 poral elements, LGTTP preserves tokens most rel- 068 evant to temporal queries while reducing compu- 069 tational requirements by 65% and maintaining 97- 070 99% of original performance. 071 Speciﬁcally, our contributions include: (i) A 072 model-agnostic framework that extracts temporal 073 cues from natural language queries to guide to- 074 ken pruning decisions. (ii) A method to inte- 075 grate LGTTP with TimeChat and LLaVA-Video 076 architectures, with particular optimization for 077 temporally-aware models. (iii) Comprehensive 078 evaluation across multiple video understanding 079 benchmarks, demonstrating that LGTTP main- 080 tains near-original performance while signiﬁcantly 081 reducing computational requirements for diverse 082 tasks. 083 1 2 Method 084 Overview and Motivation. LGTTP addresses a 085 fundamental efﬁciency challenge in VideoLLMs: 086 not all frames are equally relevant to a given 087 query, particularly for temporal understanding 088 tasks. While existing approaches either prune to- 089 kens uniformly or select entire keyframes, LGTTP 090 adaptively preserves the most temporally rele- 091 vant tokens while maintaining contextual continu- 092 ity. Our approach consists of three components: 093 temporal cue extraction from queries, temporally- 094 aware relevance prediction for different models, 095 and adaptive token pruning based on predicted 096 relevance. By leveraging temporal indicators in 097 queries, we can concentrate computational re- 098 sources on the most relevant segments. 099 Temporal Cue Extraction. Natural language 100 queries often contain rich temporal information 101 that guides our pruning strategy. Given a query 102 Q, we extract temporal information through two 103 stages: First, we identify temporal markers (e.g., 104 “before," “after," “during") using pattern matching 105 and a ﬁne-tuned classiﬁer, categorizing them into 106 Precedence, Subsequence, or Co-occurrence rela- 107 tionships. Second, we extract reference events and 108 their potential temporal positions - for example, 109 from “after talking to the coach," we identify “talk- 110 ing to the coach" as occurring earlier in the video. 111 This temporal knowledge helps prioritize frames 112 likely to contain moments of interest. 113 Adaptation to VideoLLM Architectures. 114 LGTTP integrates with various VideoLLM archi- 115 tectures according to their temporal awareness 116 capabilities. For timestamp-aware models like 117 TimeChat, we leverage existing timestamp bind- 118 ings where frame embeddings E = {e1, ..., eN} 119 already incorporate timestamp information. For 120 models using temporal instructions (e.g., LLaVA- 121 Video), we add lightweight temporal position 122 embeddings based on normalized frame positions. 123 For standard VLMs without explicit temporal 124 awareness, we introduce a temporal adapter that 125 projects frame indices into a positional embedding 126 space. 127 After adaptation, we compute relevance scores 128 by processing the query embedding eq = Ftext(Q) 129 and calculating base relevance Lbase = a · 130 cos_sim(E′, eq) + b, where a and b are learnable 131 parameters. We then incorporate extracted tempo- 132 ral cues through a weighting mechanism Ltemp = 133 Lbase ⊙Wtemp, where Wtemp prioritizes frames 134 based on identiﬁed temporal relationships. 135 Temporally-Adaptive Token Pruning. The ﬁnal 136 step converts temporal relevance scores into frame- 137 speciﬁc pruning rates. The frame-wise pruning 138 rates are computed as: 139 R = (r1, r2, ..., rN) = αN · softmax(Ltemp) (1) 140 where α controls the overall pruning rate and N 141 is the frame count. This ensures the average prun- 142 ing rate across frames is approximately α, while 143 distribution varies based on temporal relevance. 144 Critically, we employ soft selection rather than 145 hard keyframe selection. For each frame, we re- 146 tain: 147 Ti = max(Tmin, ⌈(1 −ri) · Tfull⌉) (2) 148 tokens, where Tmin is the minimum token count 149 (typically 10% of the original count Tfull). This 150 preserves contextual continuity by maintaining 151 some tokens even from less relevant frames. 152 3 Experiments 153 3.1 Experimental Setup 154 Datasets: We evaluate LGTTP across multiple 155 video understanding benchmarks: QVHighlights 156 (Lei et al.) for moment retrieval tasks with human- 157 written natural language queries; Charades-STA 158 (Gao et al., 2017) for temporal grounding that eval- 159 uates the ability to locate speciﬁc activities de- 160 scribed in text; VideoMME (Fu et al., 2024) for 161 comprehensive video question answering that tests 162 general understanding capabilities across diverse 163 scenarios; and EgoSchema (Zhang et al., 2023) 164 for egocentric video understanding with narrative- 165 style queries capturing ﬁrst-person perspectives. 166 Metrics: We use task-speciﬁc evaluation met- 167 rics aligned with standard benchmarks. TimeChat 454 (Ren et al., 2024) incorporates explicit timestamp 455 awareness by binding visual content with corre- 456 sponding timestamps, enabling accurate temporal 457 localization. LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024) 458 uses a temporal instruction preprompt to inform 459 the LLM about the video sampling process. Vide- 460 oLLaVA (Lin et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024) em- 461 ploys a learnable temporal embedding within the 462 vision encoder. While these models demonstrate 463 strong capabilities, they face computational chal- 464 lenges when processing long videos, particularly 465 for tasks requiring precise temporal understanding. 466 Other approaches like VideoChat (Li et al., 2023), 467 Vid2Seq (Yang et al., 2023), and Video-ChatGPT 468 (Maaz et al., 2024) have also shown promising 469 results in video understanding tasks but typically 470 process frames independently, making them less 471 optimal for capturing ﬁne-grained temporal rela- 472 tionships. 473 B.2 Efﬁciency Approaches for VLMs 474 Several approaches have been proposed to address 475 the computational challenges of vision token pro- 476 cessing in VLMs. Vision token pruning meth- 477 ods like PruMerge (Shang et al., 2024), ToMe 478 (Bolya et al., 2023), FastV (Chen et al., 2024), 479 Vid-TLDR (Choi et al., 2024), and DynamicViT 480 (Rao et al., 2021) focus on reducing token counts 481 based on importance metrics like attention entropy 482 or attention scores. However, these methods typ- 483 ically operate on individual frames without con- 484 sidering temporal context. Keyframe selection 485 methods like KeyVideoLLM (Liang et al., 2024), 486 VideoTree (Wang et al., 2024), and Koala (Tan 487 et al., 2024) identify and retain only the most infor- 488 mative frames, but their hard selection approach 489 disrupts temporal coherence. KVTP (Liu et al., 490 2025) bridges these approaches by using soft se- 491 lection to retain some tokens from less relevant 492 frames, but it doesn’t explicitly leverage temporal 493 cues from queries. 494 B.3 Video Understanding Benchmarks 495 The evaluation of VideoLLMs spans multiple 496 specialized benchmarks. For moment retrieval, 497 QVHighlights (Lei et al.) and Charades-STA 498 (Gao et al., 2017) are commonly used to eval- 499 uate a model’s ability to locate temporal seg- 500 ments matching natural language queries. General 501 video understanding capabilities are assessed on 502 benchmarks like VideoMME (Fu et al., 2024) and 503 EgoSchema (Zhang et al., 2023), which include di- 504 verse question-answering tasks. Step localization 505 is evaluated on datasets like NeXT-QA (Xiao et al., 506 2021) and COIN (Yansong Tang, 2019). Our ap- 507 proach aims to improve efﬁciency across this di- 508 verse range of tasks without compromising perfor- 509 mance. 510 C Implementation Details 511 We implement LGTTP by integrating it with 512 TimeChat and LLaVA-Video pipelines. For base 513 token pruning, we adopt PruMerge due to its ef- 514 fectiveness in preserving important visual infor- 515 mation, though our approach is compatible with 516 other pruning methods. The computational over- 517 head of our complete pipeline is minimal, adding 518 only 0.3-0.5% to overall inference time while re- 519 ducing computation by 65%. 520 D Temporal Marker Classiﬁcation 521 We develop our temporal marker classiﬁer without 522 manual annotation using a weakly supervised ap- 523 proach. First, we construct a comprehensive lex- 524 icon of temporal markers by extracting common 525 temporal expressions from existing NLP resources 526 (e.g., “before," “after," “during," “while," “when"). 527 We then use rule-based pattern matching to auto- 528 matically identify and classify these markers in 529 5,000 queries from QVHighlights, Charades-STA, 530 and VideoMME training sets. 531 The automatically labeled dataset is used to 532 train a 2-layer MLP classiﬁer on top of frozen 533 BERT embeddings. To improve robustness, we 534 employ data augmentation techniques including 535 synonym replacement and word reordering to cre- 536 ate variations of queries with preserved temporal 537 relationships. We also include queries without ex- 538 plicit markers as negative examples. 539 Our classiﬁer achieves 88.6% accuracy when 540 evaluated against a small manually veriﬁed test set 541 of 200 queries. For queries without explicit mark- 542 ers but containing implicit temporal references 543 6 (e.g., “show the beginning"), we rely on a prede- 544 ﬁned vocabulary of temporal terms and their rela- 545 tive positions in the video timeline. This approach 546 allows us to effectively identify temporal relation- 547 ships without requiring extensive manual annota- 548 tion. 549 7

How- 004 ever, progress in this field remains uneven 005 across languages, particularly for low-resource 006 languages like Portuguese, which lack high- 007 quality datasets. In this paper, we intro- 008 duce BRSpeech-DF, the first publicly avail- 009 able ADD dataset for Portuguese, encompass- 010 ing both Brazilian and European variants. The 011 dataset contains over 459,000 utterances, in- 012 cluding a smaller portion of real speech from 62 013 speakers and a large collection of synthetic sam- 014 ples generated using multiple zero-shot text-to- 015 speech (TTS) models, each conditioned on the 016 original speaker’s voice. By providing this re- 017 source, our objective is to support the develop- 018 ment of robust, multilingual detection systems, 019 thereby advancing equity in speech forensics 020 and security research. BRSpeech-DF addresses 021 a significant gap in annotated data for underrep- 022 resented languages, facilitating more inclusive 023 and generalizable advancements in synthetic 024 speech detection. 025 Our dataset and codes are publicly available1. 026 1 Introduction 027 The increasing sophistication of generative mod- 028 els has resulted in a proliferation of highly realis- 029 tic synthetic media (Xie et al., 2025), including 030 speech deepfakes. While such technologies of- 031 fer promising opportunities for accessibility and 032 human-computer interaction, they also pose signifi- 033 cant threats to societal trust, privacy, and security 034 (Kharvi, 2024). This paper presents a data se- 005 lection methodology specifically designed for 006 fine-tuning machine translation systems, which 007 leverages the synergy between a learner model 008 and a pre-trained reference model to enhance 009 overall training effectiveness. By defining a 010 learnability score, our approach systematically 011 evaluates the utility of data points for training, 012 ensuring that only the most relevant and im- 013 pactful examples contribute to the fine-tuning 014 process. Furthermore, our method employs 015 a batch selection strategy which considers in- 016 terdependencies among data points, optimiz- 017 ing the efficiency of the training process while 018 maintaining a focus on data relevance. Experi- 019 ments on English-to-Persian translation using 020 an mBART model fine-tuned on the CCMatrix 021 dataset demonstrate that our method achieves 022 a fivefold improvement in data efficiency com- 023 pared to an iid baseline. Experimental results 024 indicate that our approach improves computa- 025 tional efficiency by 24% when utilizing cached 026 embeddings, as it requires fewer training data 027 points. Additionally, it enhances generalization, 028 resulting in superior translation performance 029 compared to iid methods. 030 1 Introduction 031 Machine translation is a fundamental task in natural 032 language processing. As with any data-driven learn- 033 ing task, the effectiveness of training heavily de- 034 pends on the quality of the data. (Fenza et al., 2021; 035 Gupta et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021) In particular, 036 parallel datasets may contain irrelevant sentence 037 pairs or poorly translated documents, which nega- 038 tively impact the performance of the final model. 039 Beyond the quality of data, the state of the 040 learner model itself plays a crucial role in select- 041 ing beneficial training data.
